grammatical_complexity.notes: Dominated by simple present and going-to future typical of dialogue. Present perfect appears several times (I've cleaned, I've put away, I've done). One second conditional (If he stopped... he would run out of time) and a few first conditionals. Complex structures are a noticeable minority but not dominant.

cultural_reference_load.notes: Santa Claus is globally known, but specific North American traditions (eggnog, coal in stocking, leaving food for reindeer, mall Santa) add comprehension weight. Cribbage and glögg are niche. Plot is followable without deep cultural knowledge but nuances are missed.

sentence_structure.notes: Dialogue format with short conversational exchanges. Mostly subject-verb-object. Occasional compound sentences with 'and', 'but', 'so'. A few longer sentences with subordinate clauses but average remains low.

items.reason: Context (not paying attention to the kids) makes the meaning clear enough, though a Spanish speaker might initially think 'not know.'
Used as a frequency adverb; context makes it unambiguous. Spanish 'once' (eleven) doesn't fit here.

Spanish 'pretender' means 'to attempt/try to.' A Spanish speaker could read 'pretend to sleep' as 'try to sleep,' which would cause genuine confusion since the girls are faking sleep, not trying to fall asleep.
Used playfully in a clear context; Spanish 'test' is borrowed from English and means the same thing.
